findings.title: Lemma3.8's unrestricted time range is false
findings.source_locator: Lemma3.8 pp.1841-1842; constant(3.2) p.1834; small-delta use pp.1843-1845.
findings.common_hypotheses_tex:
\section{Identity, assumptions, and review scope}
The reviewed paper is Rami Atar, \emph{A weak formulation of free boundary problems and its application to hydrodynamic limits of particle systems with selection}, \emph{Annals of Probability} 53(5) (2025), 1825--1856, DOI \url{10.1214/24-AOP1751} \cite{atar}. The frozen author-hosted journal PDF has 32 pages. All its definitions, statements, proofs and references were read. Page numbers below are journal page numbers; PDF page \(k\) is page \(1824+k\).

The individual diffusion has bounded coefficients \(b,c\), with \(b\in C^1\), \(c\in C^2\), bounded \(c'\), and \(c\) bounded away from zero. Its branching rate is \(\kappa\geq0\), and its forward operator is
\[
L^*u=\partial_x^2(au)-\partial_x(bu)+\kappa u,\qquad a=c^2/2.
\]
The initial measure \(\xi_0\) is any probability measure, including an atomic one. The injection measure \(\alpha\) is nonnegative and locally finite in time. Its cumulative mass \(I\) satisfies either the spatial domination condition \(\alpha(dx,dt)\leq C\,dx\,dI_t\) with positive temporal H\"older regularity, or temporal H\"older regularity strictly greater than \(1/2\). The removal mass \(J\) is nondecreasing, absolutely continuous, H\"older continuous with a positive exponent and zero at zero. The mass equation
\[
m_t=1+\kappa\int_0^t m_s\,ds+I_t-J_t
\]
has a strictly positive global lower bound. The stochastic primitives satisfy the independence and adapted martingale requirements (S.6)--(S.7), and their normalized data converge in probability as in Assumption 2.3.

The weak formulation couples \(\partial_tu-L^*u=\alpha-\beta\) with \(\beta(\R\times[0,t])=J_t\), nonnegativity, and
\[
\beta\{(x,t):U(x,t)>0\}=0,\qquad
U(x,t)=\int_{-\infty}^x u(y,t)\,dy.
\]
This orientation describes removal on the \emph{left}. Absolute continuity of \(J\) is operative: it makes this condition invariant under changing a density on a Lebesgue-null set of times.
findings.complete_evidence_tex:
\begin{problem}[Minor: Lemma 3.8 needs a small-time restriction]
Lemma 3.8, pp.~1841--1842, is stated for every \(\delta>0\), but its proof uses (3.2), p.~1834, which is established only for times at most one. Its unrestricted statement is false.
\end{problem}
\begin{proof}
Take \(b=1\), \(c=1\), \(\kappa>0\), no injection, and \(J_t=\kappa t\). Put
\[
\lambda=\sqrt{2\kappa},\qquad v=1+\lambda,\qquad
q(z)=2\kappa z e^{-\lambda z}\mathbf1_{\{z\geq0\}},
\]
and define
\[
u(x,t)=q(x-vt),\quad \xi_0(dx)=q(x)\,dx,\quad
\beta(dx,dt)=\kappa\delta_{vt}(dx)\,dt.
\]
These are admissible data with \(m_t=1\). In particular, \(J\) is Lipschitz and the first injection alternative holds trivially for \(\alpha=0\).
Direct calculation gives
\[
\int q=1,\qquad
\tfrac12q''+(v-1)q'+\kappa q=0\quad(z>0),\qquad
\tfrac12q'(0)=\kappa.
\]
Since \(q(0)=0\), the distributional boundary term is precisely
\(-\kappa\delta_{vt}\); thus this pair solves the weak equation and complementarity condition.

For the drift-one Brownian diffusion,
\(\int_{-\infty}^x p_t(x,y)\,dy=\Phi(-\sqrt t)\).
Hence \(c_*=\Phi(-1)\) is a valid constant in (3.2), and set \(C_*=2/c_*\), the constant denoted \(c^*\) in Lemma 3.8. For \(n=2\),
\[
j_2(\delta)=e^{\kappa\delta}-1,\qquad
\rho_{2,\delta}=2v\delta.
\]
Let \(F(z)=1-(1+z)e^{-z}\), the distribution function of a unit-rate Gamma distribution of shape two. When
\(p=C_*(e^{\kappa\delta}-1)<1\), the lemma's domain condition holds, but its proposed bound is
\[
\Lambda_p(u_\delta)=v\delta+\frac{F^{-1}(p)}{\sqrt{2\kappa}}.
\]
For \(\kappa=10^{-4}\), \(\delta=100\), independent high-precision evaluation gives
\[
p=0.1266918912,\qquad
\rho_{2,\delta}=202.8284271,\qquad
\Lambda_p(u_\delta)=144.8644698.
\]
The claimed inequality is reversed by about \(57.964\).
This is not dependent on an optimized choice of \(c_*\): for any fixed valid \(c_*>0\), take \(\kappa\delta=h\) small enough that \(C_*(e^h-1)<1\), then let \(\kappa\downarrow0\). The boundary displacement grows like \(\kappa^{-1}\), whereas the quantile offset grows like \(\kappa^{-1/2}\).
\end{proof}
\emph{Counterevidence and impact.}
Proposition 3.7 uses Lemma 3.8 only for sufficiently small \(\delta\), and uniqueness takes \(\delta\downarrow0\). Restricting Lemma 3.8 to \(0<\delta\leq1\) repairs the displayed proof without changing that limit argument. Alternatively a constant depending on a specified time horizon can be used. The example disproves the unrestricted lemma, not Theorem 3.1.

findings.complete_evidence_tex:
\begin{problem}[Minor: the \(v\)-bound in Lemma 3.3(iii) is too general]
On p.~1835, \(v\) is defined in part (i) using an arbitrary measure \(\gamma\) whose cumulative mass has some positive H\"older exponent. Part (iii)'s assertion
\(v\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty);L^\infty)\) does not follow for that \(v\).
\end{problem}
Take standard Brownian motion, \(\kappa=0\), any probability initial measure, and
\[
\gamma(dx,ds)=\delta_0(dx)(1-s)^{-3/4}\mathbf1_{(0,1)}(s)\,ds.
\]
Its cumulative mass is
\(K_t=4[1-(1-t)_+^{1/4}]\), a nondecreasing \(1/4\)-H\"older function starting at zero. For \(t=1-\varepsilon\), \(|x|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1/3\), retaining only \(r=t-s\in[\varepsilon,2\varepsilon]\) gives
\begin{equation}
(S*\gamma)(x,1-\varepsilon)
\geq
\frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt2\,3^{3/4}}\,
\varepsilon^{-1/4}.
\end{equation}
Thus the essential supremum is unbounded near time one. This is a positive-measure phenomenon, not just an infinite value at a single point.

\emph{Counterevidence and repair.}
The proof on p.~1836 estimates \(S_t\xi_0+S*\alpha\), using the stronger admissibility alternatives for \(\alpha\). The \(v\) actually used in Lemmas 4.3--4.4 is explicitly this latter function. Setting \(v=S_t\xi_0+S*\alpha\) in part (iii), or adding the same admissibility conditions on \(\gamma\), removes the overstatement. The example does not refute the boundedness of that intended dominating density or part (i)'s \(L^1_tL^q_x\) assertion.

\section{Boundary orientation and initial time}

findings.complete_evidence_tex:
\begin{problem}[Minor: Remark 2.6(i) identifies the opposite selection boundary]
Remark 2.6(i), p.~1833, states that a classical solution of (1.2) produces a solution of (2.10) by taking \(\beta(dx,dt)=c_0\delta_{\ell_t}(dx)\,dt\). This is incompatible with the left-tail complementarity condition.
\end{problem}
For a concrete classical solution of (1.2), p.~1826, set \(c_0=1\), \(\ell_t=1\) and
\(u(x,t)=2(1-x)\) on \(0\leq x\leq1\), zero for \(x\geq1\), with this stationary initial density. It has mass one, zero second derivative in the interior and both specified flux values equal to one. If the density is extended by zero to \(x<0\), then
\[
U(1,t)=\int_{-\infty}^1u(x,t)\,dx=1,\qquad
\beta\{U>0\}\big|_{\R\times[0,T]}=T>0.
\]
Hence the proposed pair fails (2.10)(ii).

\emph{Counterevidence and repair.}
Equation (1.2) deliberately removes the \emph{rightmost} particle and includes reflection at the origin; the main model removes the leftmost particle on the full line. A corresponding weak formulation must use the right tail and the appropriate half-line boundary flux, or explicitly transform the orientation and domain. Merely extending the half-line density by zero also introduces a distributional issue at the reflecting endpoint. The general idea of a complementary weak formulation remains useful; this direct identification with (1.2) is the incorrect statement.

findings.complete_evidence_tex:
\begin{problem}[Minor: three transcription errors in Lemma 4.1's martingale derivation]
The formulas on pp.~1846--1847 require an indicator reversal, removal of an extra branching-rate factor, and retention of the terminal configuration term before setting \(t=T\).
\end{problem}
The definition after (4.3) prints
\(\mathbf1_{\{\sigma^i\geq t\}}\int_{\sigma^i}^{t\wedge\tau^i}c\,\partial_x\phi\,dB^i\).
For an initial particle \(\sigma^i=0\), this is zero for every \(t>0\), whereas the preceding It\^o integral is generally nonzero. For instance, take standard Brownian motion, no events on a short interval and a compactly supported test function with nonzero spatial derivative near the initial point. The correct indicator is \(\mathbf1_{\{t\geq\sigma^i\}}\).

Next, the printed definition
\(M_t^{\#,N}=\sum_i\int_{\sigma^i}^{t\wedge\tau^i}d\widehat\pi_s^i\)
gives
\[
Y_t^N=\kappa\int_0^t m_s^N\,ds+M_t^{\#,N},
\]
not (4.5)'s expression with \(\kappa M_t^{\#,N}\).
With one initial particle, \(\kappa=2\), and no births or removals up to \(t\), the defined martingale equals \(-2t\). The printed right side is then \(2t-4t=-2t\), while \(Y_t^N=0\).

Finally, the finite-time sum at the bottom of p.~1846 requires
\[
\int_{\R\times[0,t]}\phi\,d\bar\beta^N
=\langle\phi_0,\bar\xi_0^N\rangle
+\int_{\R\times[0,t]}\phi\,d\bar\alpha^N
+\int_0^t\langle\partial_s\phi+L\phi,\bar\xi_s^N\rangle ds
+\bar M_t^N-\langle\phi_t,\bar\xi_t^N\rangle.
\]
The last term is omitted in the displayed expression.

\emph{Counterevidence and repair.}
The next page explicitly sets \(t=T\), where \(\phi_T=0\), and the quadratic-variation argument already uses the correct lifetime orientation. Correcting these three formulas restores the usual decomposition and its order \(N^{-1}\) quadratic variation. No failure of Lemma 4.1's vanishing-noise conclusion is established.

findings.complete_evidence_tex:
\begin{problem}[Major: the imported linear well-posedness argument lacks its required hypotheses]
The passage following (2.9), p.~1833, transforms the forward operator using
\(\bar b=-b+a'\) and \(\bar\kappa=\kappa-b'\), then invokes Amann's Theorems 1 and 13 and Remarks 1 and 2(b). The paper's assumptions do not imply the explicit coefficient bounds in that reference.
\end{problem}
The acquired original \cite{amann}, p.~105, assumes bounded uniformly smooth coefficients in its general elliptic operator; Remark 2(b), p.~116, explicitly permits a bounded measurable zeroth-order coefficient. But \(b(x)=\sin(x^2)\), \(c=1\) satisfy Assumption 2.1, while
\[
\bar\kappa(x)=\kappa-2x\cos(x^2)
\]
is unbounded. Thus the stated transformation does not by itself verify the cited sufficient conditions. The reference also mentions further relaxations; those should not be silently identified with the assumptions here.

\emph{A direct repair under the original assumptions.}
The underlying linear statement can instead be justified without a bound on \(b'\).
Let \(h=|c|\), set
\[
y=F(x)=\int_0^x h(r)^{-1}\,dr,\qquad
w(y,t)=h(x)u(x,t),\quad x=F^{-1}(y).
\]
This is a global bi-Lipschitz change of variable, preserving the \(L^1_tL^q_x\) class for every finite \(q>1\). Applying the chain rule in the weak formulation, justified by local smooth approximation of tests, gives
\[
\partial_tw=\tfrac12\partial_y^2w-\partial_y(Bw)+\kappa w+\nu,
\quad
B(y)=\frac{b(x)}{h(x)}-\frac12h'(x),
\]
where \(B\) is bounded and \(\nu\) is the pushforward of the driving measure. Include the pushed initial measure at time zero in a measure \(\eta\).
With \(G\) the standard heat kernel, the equation has the distributional Duhamel form
\begin{equation}
w=G*\eta-(\partial_yG)*(Bw)+\kappa G*w.
\end{equation}
The measure term belongs to \(L^1([0,T];L^q)\), since
\(\|G_t\|_q=C_qt^{-(q-1)/(2q)}\) and the exponent is less than one.
The remaining linear operator is a contraction in the equivalent norm
\(\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|w_t\|_qdt\) for sufficiently large \(\lambda\), because
\[
\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|\partial_yG_t\|_1dt
\leq C\lambda^{-1/2},\qquad
\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|G_t\|_1dt\leq\lambda^{-1}.
\]
Heat-equation duality gives the same Duhamel identity for any distributional solution in this class. The contraction therefore supplies existence and uniqueness there; transforming back gives the needed linear result. Compatibility across \(q\) follows by performing the construction simultaneously in intersections of these spaces.

\emph{Dependency and severity.}
This repair addresses the imported linear uniqueness used to identify the mild version in Lemma 3.3 and the limit equation in Section 4. It explains why a citation-hypothesis mismatch should not be presented as a counterexample to the main theorem. A precise applicable reference or the direct argument should replace the unsupported application. The displayed invocation does not establish linear well-posedness for the stated coefficient class; Lemma 3.3 then uses this unsupported uniqueness to identify the mild representative, on which the barrier proof and limit identification depend. This is a Major gap in a core derivation. The direct argument above supplies a repair under the original assumptions; it does not turn the original invocation into a valid one or establish that the final theorem is false.
